n0001.title: Towards a Theory of Bugs
n0001.gist: Bugs are unavoidable in any program that does real computation, because such programs can always do things we cannot foresee.
n0001.question: Theory of bugs — why do even very simple programs have bugs we cannot rule out? (an argument with examples)

n0002.title: My Program Did the Wrong Thing!
n0002.gist: Bugs appear even in very simple programs, and unpredictable computation explains why neither humans nor automated tools can fully root them out.
n0002.question: Bugs — why can't we expect to root them out entirely? (a framing argument)

n0013.title: Bugs in Turing Machines
n0013.gist: Simple Turing machines that seem to compute n + 1 can fail suddenly at larger inputs, and such late failures are common.
n0013.question: Turing machines — how long can a bug stay hidden in a tiny program? (worked examples)

n0046.title: What Counts as a Bug?
n0046.gist: A bug is a mismatch with a simpler specification, whether a rival program, a forbidden behavior or a required property, and every kind of specification gets escaped.
n0046.question: Specification — how is a bug defined, and why does it always slip through? (several kinds of specification)

n0071.title: Telling If a Bug Will Occur
n0071.gist: Cellular automata doubling their input show that simple pictures prove correctness, complex ones raise doubt, and formal proofs help only in pockets and bring no advantage over running.
n0071.question: Detecting bugs — how far can looking at behavior or proofs rule bugs out? (cellular automaton examples and proofs)

n0072.title: A Cellular Automaton Example
n0072.gist: Cellular automata built to double a block of cells also show late bugs, appearing at sizes such as 14, 24 or 32 after seeming to work.

n0086.title: Can One Tell If There's Going to Be a Bug?
n0086.gist: Visual simplicity guarantees no bugs, and one complicated-looking rule can be shown bug-free by analysis of its inner pattern, but fluctuating cases offer no guarantee.

n0120.title: But What about Formal Proofs?
n0120.gist: Symbolic axioms and induction can prove that simple Turing machines always compute n + 1, but buggy machines yield no proof and proving costs as much as running.

n0168.title: Computational Irreducibility and Bugs
n0168.gist: Bugs ultimately come from computational irreducibility: useful programs must hold unforeseeable behavior, with only pockets of predictability where we can guarantee some properties.
n0168.question: Computational irreducibility — why does it make bugs fundamentally unavoidable? (an argument)

n0179.title: Did I Test Enough Cases?
n0179.gist: Testing by sampling cannot give certainty, since bugs can be arbitrarily rare and rare phenomena keep turning up whenever ruliology samples more exhaustively.
n0179.question: Ruliological induction — why does testing many cases fail to show a program is correct?

n0191.title: Surprises and Mathematical Bugs
n0191.gist: Ruliology is full of sudden surprises that act like bugs, and mathematics has counterexamples too but mostly stays in pockets of reducibility.
n0191.question: Surprises — how common are bug-like surprises in ruliology and mathematics? (many examples)

n0192.title: Some Typical Ruliological Surprises
n0192.gist: Rule 30, rare Turing machines, a cellular automaton changing at input 97,439 and a combinator halting after 137,356,329 steps show that long-quiet systems can suddenly surprise.

n0224.title: Mathematical “Bugs”
n0224.gist: Mathematics has counterexamples like the coefficient 2 in x^105 – 1, but pure mathematics rarely meets them because it stays in human-level pockets of reducibility.

n0239.title: Bugs in Practice
n0239.gist: Good language design and seeing inside a computation help most, but deeper bugs remain for any program doing irreducible work, including AI-trained ones.
n0239.question: Bugs in practice — how should we write and check programs given irreducible bugs? (practical advice)
